**Practice.** Go down the list. Then pick the two weakest keys on it and give them ten minutes, hands together, quietly. Then play the piece you finished, once, for pleasure.
Pieces, finished — what this stage is:
Four stages of preparation. This one is playing music, and the discipline in it is finishing.

**The change.** Stages 1 to 4 taught technique and reading with pieces attached. Stage 5 inverts that: pieces are the work, and technique arrives because a piece demands it. At this point more preparation is the thing holding you back.

**The rule of the stage: a piece is finished or it does not count.** Finished means playable start to end, at a tempo that sounds like the music, without stopping, without a bar you dread, with the phrasing and dynamics in it and the fingering settled.

**Why that rule.** Half-learned pieces are the single commonest way self-taught playing stalls. They feel like progress, they accumulate, none of them is playable for anyone, and the hard bar in each one gets practised wrong every time it is played. Five finished pieces are worth twenty started.

**How many: five, over this stage.** Three classical, in three different styles, and two off the shelf. That is the set, and the last lesson of the stage lists candidates.

**Pick slightly above your level.** A piece you can already nearly play teaches nothing; a piece four grades up teaches nothing either, because it never gets finished. Slightly beyond — one or two bars that look impossible on day one — is where the learning is.

**Interleave the pieces.** Do not learn them in sequence. Two or three at once, at different stages of completion, rotated through a session. It feels slower and it is faster, which is stage 3's finding applied to repertoire.

**Keep the daily ten minutes of sight-reading** going underneath all of it, separate from the pieces, below your level, as it has been since stage 2.

**What this stage is not.** It is not a grade syllabus and there is no exam at the end of it. The pieces are chosen because they teach something and because they are worth playing.

**What to listen for, across the whole stage:** whether a piece sounds like music to you when you play it. Not perfect — like music. That is the test of finished.

**Practice.** Read the last lesson of this stage now, choose your first classical piece and your first piece off the shelf, and start the classical one today.
Choosing a piece you can actually finish:
The most consequential decision in learning a piece is made before you play a note, and it is usually made badly.

**Judge a score before you commit to it.** Open it and look for these, in this order:

1. **How many notes at once.** Two single lines is easy; four-note chords in both hands is not.
2. **The fastest thing in it.** Find the shortest note value and imagine playing it at the marked tempo. Semiquaver runs at Allegro are a different piece from the same notes at Andante.
3. **The key.** Up to two accidentals is comfortable now; five is a reading project on top of a playing one.
4. **How far the hands move.** Leaps, hand crossings and anything above two octaves of travel per bar.
5. **How long it is.** A page is a few weeks. Four pages is a season.
6. **The hardest bar.** Find it — there is always one — and be honest about whether you can imagine playing it at all.

**If the hardest bar looks impossible, that is the right piece.** If three bars look impossible, it is the wrong one.

**Grade numbers are a rough guide and they are not interchangeable.** ABRSM and RCM grades do not line up with each other, and MuseScore's difficulty labels are the uploader's opinion. Use them to narrow a search, never to decide.

**Arrangement, not piece.** "Merry-Go-Round of Life" exists at beginner level and at concert level under the same title. Difficulty is a fact about the arrangement in front of you.

**Hearing it first is allowed and is useful.** Find a recording, listen once, then look at the score. Knowing how it goes makes reading it faster and makes mistakes audible. What is not useful is learning it entirely by copying a video — that is two lessons from here.

**The honest signal that you chose wrong**: two weeks in and the piece is not noticeably better than it was in week one. Put it aside, pick something simpler, come back in six months. That is not failure, it is the same piece at a better time.

**What to listen for:** whether you want to play it. A piece you do not like will not get the forty repetitions it needs.

**Practice.** Take the piece you think you want next. Go down the six checks above with the score in front of you, out loud, and find its hardest bar before you play anything.
Where the free scores are, and which edi:
All of this material is free. Some of it is badly presented, and knowing the difference saves weeks.

**IMSLP** has essentially every public-domain score — every piece of classical music whose composer died long enough ago. For everything in this stage that is all of it.

**What to look for in an IMSLP edition:**

- **A clean, typeset score** rather than a scan of a nineteenth-century print. Many pieces have both; the typeset ones are usually recent engravings uploaded by volunteers.
- **Editorial fingerings**, which are genuinely useful at this stage even when you later disagree with them.
- **An urtext or urtext-like edition** for the music itself: it prints what the composer wrote. Heavily edited nineteenth-century editions add dynamics, pedalling and slurs the composer never wrote, often with no indication of what was added.
- **Readable size.** A scan photographed at an angle, with four systems to a page and bleed-through from the other side, is a reading problem on top of a playing one. There is almost always a better scan of the same piece.

**What to avoid:** first-edition facsimiles with old clefs or old note spellings, and "complete works" volumes where your piece sits in six-point type.

**MuseScore** is where the shelf lives — community arrangements of anime, game and pop music, often several per song at different difficulties. Viewing scores in the browser is free; downloading and printing some of them wants an account or a subscription, and playing from the screen works fine. Arrangement quality varies enormously, so check the comments and prefer uploads with many views.

**Ultimate Guitar** for chord charts. No notation, just chords over lyrics, and that is exactly what you want for a cover you will arrange yourself.

**Print it, or at least do not scroll it.** A piece being learned wants to be on paper where you can pencil fingerings in. A tablet that does not scroll works too. A phone does not.

**Pencil, always.** Fingerings, the hard bars circled, the sections marked. A clean score after two weeks of work means you have not been marking up, which means you have been re-deciding.

**Practice.** Find your chosen piece on IMSLP. Compare two editions of it side by side and pick one on the criteria above. Print it. Then find your shelf piece on MuseScore and compare two arrangements.
The learning sequence, as a checklist:
Everything stages 2 to 4 taught about learning a piece, in the order it is done. This is the routine for every piece from here on.

**Before the keyboard:**

1. **Listen once.** Then put the recording away.
2. **Name the key**, from the signature and the last bass note.
3. **Mark the sections.** Usually four or eight bars each, ending where a phrase breathes.
4. **Mark the scale fragments and the arpeggios.** Finger them from the scales you know.
5. **Mark the accidentals outside the key**, and work out what each one is doing.
6. **Find the hardest bar** and circle it.
7. **Write the fingerings in**, everywhere you had to think.

**At the keyboard, per section:**

8. **Hands separately, slowly**, until each hand is automatic by the talking test.
9. **Hands together at half tempo**, listening for the two hands arriving as one.
10. **The hardest bar as a fragment**, on its own, many times, slowly.
11. **The joins** — the last note of one section into the first of the next — as their own fragments.
12. **Up to tempo in small steps**, dropping back the moment it stops being even.

**Then the music:**

13. **Phrasing.** Where each line breathes.
14. **Dynamics.** Written and implied.
15. **Balance.** Melody above accompaniment, every time.
16. **Start to end, no stopping**, as its own practised skill.

**Interleave throughout.** Not section 1 to completion then section 2 — rotate, which means rotating between sections at different states of readiness.

**One named fault per repetition**, always. "The left hand is late on beat three", never "play it better".

**The order matters more than it looks.** Shaping a phrase before the notes are secure teaches an unsecured phrase. Playing start to end before the hard bar works teaches a stumble at that bar, forty times.

**This takes a few weeks per piece** at this level and that is the correct speed. A piece learned in three days is a piece learned approximately.

**What to listen for:** whichever single thing the step says. Listening for everything at once is listening for nothing.

**Practice.** Do steps 1 to 7 on your chosen piece, with a pencil, before touching the keys. Then step 8 on the first section only.
Sectioning, and practising out of order:
A piece is not learned from the beginning. It is learned in pieces, and the order is a decision.

**Section it on the music's own joints.** Phrase ends, repeat signs, the double bar where the second idea starts. Four or eight bars is typical; a section should be short enough to hold in your head whole.

**Number the sections in pencil.** They become the unit you talk about — "section 4 is late on the second beat" — and they are what you rotate between.

**Start with the hardest section, not the first.** The reason is arithmetic: whatever you start with gets the most repetitions, and in a piece learned front to back that is the opening, which is usually the easiest part. That is why so much amateur playing is strong for sixteen bars and collapses.

**So the order is roughly:** hardest section first, then the other difficult ones, then the easy ones, then the joins, then the whole.

**The joins are their own sections.** The last two notes of one plus the first two of the next, practised as a four-note fragment. A piece made of fluent sections and unpractised joins stops four times.

**Chaining, when a section resists.** Learn the last bar of it. Then the second-to-last plus the last. Then three bars. Always ending where you have already been, so you are always playing towards something secure rather than towards something unknown. This is backward chaining and it is the strongest tool in this lesson.

**Rotate, do not grind.** Section 3 for five minutes, section 1 for five, section 5 for five, then section 3 again — rather than twenty minutes of section 3. It feels less productive in the session and tests better the next day.

**Keep a written note of which sections are where.** Three states is enough: not yet, hands separately, together. A piece with eight sections and no notes gets practised according to mood, which means the hard ones get avoided.

**Playing the whole piece has its own practice.** Once the sections are solid, "start to end without stopping" is a separate skill and needs its own repetitions — being able to play all eight sections is not the same as playing them in a row.

**What to listen for:** at the joins, a hesitation. It is the commonest fault in a piece that is otherwise learned.

**Practice.** Number the sections of your piece in pencil. Mark which is hardest. Work that one today, by backward chaining, and nothing else.
Baroque: the first classical piece, and:
The first of three classical pieces, and the style that teaches the most per note.

**What Baroque writing is**, at the keyboard: two or more independent lines, both of them tunes, with the harmony arising from how they fit together. Not melody over accompaniment — that comes later historically and in this stage.

**What it wants from you:**

- **Clarity above everything.** Every note audible and in its place. This style is unforgiving of mush and that is why it teaches so well.
- **Finger legato, no pedal.** The connection between notes is made by the fingers holding and releasing precisely. Baroque keyboards had no sustain pedal; the music does not need one and sounds wrong with it.
- **Terraced dynamics, not gradual ones.** A harpsichord cannot crescendo, so the style shapes by section — this passage louder, that one softer — rather than by swelling through a phrase. On a piano, a modest swell is acceptable and fashionable; a Romantic one is not.
- **Both hands equal.** The left hand is a line with its own shape, not an accompaniment to be tucked away. This is where stage 3's independence work pays.
- **Steady tempo.** Very little rubato. The pulse is the frame the counterpoint hangs on.
- **Ornaments are optional at first.** Trills and mordents printed in the score may be left out while learning and added once the notes are secure. Leaving them out permanently is a loss; leaving them out for now is sensible.

**The candidates**, all free on IMSLP:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Petzold — Minuet in G, BWV Anh. 114** | the standard first piece, and deservedly |
| **Petzold — Minuet in G minor, BWV Anh. 115** | its companion, a little harder, minor key |
| **Bach — Little Prelude in C, BWV 939** | short, patterned, teaches evenness |
| **Bach — Prelude in C, BWV 846** | broken chords throughout, every bar the same shape, very satisfying |
| **Bach — Minuet in G, BWV Anh. 116** | the third minuet, less played |

**The recommendation: a minuet first, then BWV 939.** The minuets teach two-voice independence; the prelude teaches evenness and hand position.

**What to listen for:** whether the left-hand line is as shaped as the right. Play the left hand alone and ask whether it sounds like a tune. In this music it should.

**Practice.** Choose one. Do the full checklist on it. Give it three or four weeks and finish it.
Classical: the sonatina, and tempo disci:
The second style. Where Baroque was two lines, the Classical period is melody over accompaniment — which is the texture most of the music you want to play uses.

**What Classical writing wants:**

- **A clean, singing right hand** over a quiet, regular left. The balance work from stage 3, applied for an entire piece.
- **Alberti bass and its relatives.** Broken-chord accompaniment, note after note, which must be absolutely even and absolutely in the background.
- **Precise articulation.** Staccato means staccato, slurs mean exactly the notes under them. The style's character is in those marks and ignoring them flattens it.
- **Tempo discipline.** Classical music is measured. A phrase may breathe, but the pulse holds, and the commonest amateur fault is slowing down at anything difficult — which is audible, and is a different thing from rubato.
- **Scales and arpeggios, literally.** This is the repertoire stage 4 was for: a Clementi sonatina is largely scales and broken chords, fingered as the scales you practise.
- **Classical dynamics are structural.** Loud at the start of a section, soft at the answering phrase. Shape by phrase rather than by note.

**The candidates**, all free on IMSLP:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Clementi — Sonatina Op. 36 No. 1, 1st movement** | the standard, three short movements, modulates to G |
| **Clementi — Sonatina Op. 36 No. 1, 2nd movement** | slow, lyrical, the balance test |
| **Beethoven — Sonatina in G, Anh. 5, 1st movement** | attribution doubtful, piece lovely |
| **Kuhlau — Sonatina Op. 55 No. 1** | a step up from Clementi, same shape |
| **Mozart — Minuet in F, K. 2** | written when he was six; short and genuinely approachable |

**The recommendation: Clementi Op. 36 No. 1.** It is the conventional first sonatina for good reason — the first movement is a complete piece of Classical form in about forty bars, and the left hand teaches Alberti bass as well as anything written.

**Keep the metronome on for part of every session with this piece.** Classical tempo discipline is a measurable thing and the metronome is how you measure it. Then play without it, so the pulse comes from you.

**What to listen for:** the left hand being audibly quieter and perfectly even. If the Alberti bass is the loudest thing in the bar, the piece sounds like an exercise.

**Practice.** Choose one. Checklist, hardest section first. Give it a month, interleaved with the Baroque piece rather than after it.
Romantic: the singing tone:
The third style, and the one most people mean when they say they want to play the piano.

**What Romantic writing wants:**

- **A melody that sings.** Long lines, played with the arm rather than the fingers, each note connected to the next. The tone comes from weight arriving slowly rather than from force.
- **Rubato.** The pulse bends — a little time taken at the top of a phrase, a little given back. Not slowing down because something is hard; a deliberate stretch inside a tempo you otherwise keep.
- **Big dynamic range**, and gradual. Crescendos that last eight bars. This is where the piano does what no harpsichord could, which is why the music is written this way.
- **Rich textures** — chords, wide left-hand spans, the melody often inside the hand rather than on top. Stage 3's voicing work is what makes that possible.
- **The pedal.** Which is stage 6, and which is the honest limitation of doing Romantic music now.

**So choose Romantic pieces that survive without pedal.** Most teaching pieces of the period do, because they were written for children who had to learn the notes first. Burgmüller and Schumann are the obvious answer.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Burgmüller — La Candeur, Op. 100 No. 1** | written to teach a singing right hand |
| **Burgmüller — Arabesque, Op. 100 No. 2** | A minor, scale runs, sounds far harder than it is |
| **Burgmüller — Innocence, Op. 100 No. 5** | melody and simple accompaniment |
| **Schumann — Melody, Op. 68 No. 1** | four-part writing, the voicing test |
| **Schumann — Soldier's March, Op. 68 No. 2** | rhythmic, crisp, no pedal needed at all |
| **Tchaikovsky — Old French Song, Op. 39 No. 16** | a genuinely beautiful tune, very few notes |

**The recommendation: Burgmüller's Arabesque**, if you want the clearest possible payoff from stage 4, or **Tchaikovsky's Old French Song** if you want the most music for the fewest notes.

**Rubato, practically.** Learn the piece strictly in time first. Then take time at the one or two places where the line reaches its highest point, and give it back immediately after. Rubato applied before the piece is secure is indistinguishable from not being able to play it.

**These pieces come back in stage 6** with the pedal, and they will sound like different pieces. That is not a reason to wait.

**What to listen for:** whether the melody's long notes stay alive. A sung line does not sag in the middle; on a piano that means the next note arrives before the last has died.

**Practice.** Choose one. Play its melody alone, right hand, with the arm, listening only to tone — before any work on the left hand at all.
Modern and still: playing slowly on purp:
One more style, and the one that proves playing well is not about playing hard things.

**What this music is.** Satie, Debussy's easier pieces, Einaudi, and most of the film and game writing you like: slow tempos, few notes, enormous space, and all the difficulty in tone and timing rather than in execution.

**Why it belongs in this stage.** A beginner can play the notes of Gymnopédie No. 1 within a week. Playing it so that it sounds like the recording takes much longer, and what takes the time is exactly what the other styles also need — even tone, controlled quiet playing, steady slow tempo, and the nerve to leave a silence alone.

**What it wants:**

- **Quiet playing, under control.** Much harder than loud. A piano played softly exposes every unevenness.
- **A very steady slow pulse.** Slow music has nowhere to hide a wobble, and there is no momentum carrying you.
- **Space.** Rests played as rests, not hurried through. The commonest fault in this music is impatience.
- **Voicing**, since the melody often sits inside a chord.

**The honest limitation: much of it wants the pedal.** Gymnopédie No. 1 without pedal is thin, because the left hand's bass note is meant to ring under the chord. You can play it now with finger legato and it will be worth playing; it becomes the real thing in stage 6.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Satie — Gymnopédie No. 1** | free on IMSLP; wants pedal, still worth it |
| **Satie — Gnossienne No. 1** | slow, modal, hypnotic |
| **Schumann — First Loss, Op. 68 No. 16** | not modern, same virtues, no pedal needed |
| **Film and game themes** | from MuseScore — mostly this texture exactly |

**The recommendation: play one of these now and keep it for life.** It is the piece you will play when someone asks you to play something, long before the hard repertoire is ready.

**Resist speeding up.** The pull towards tempo in slow music is strong because slow playing feels exposed. Use the metronome at the marked tempo and stay there.

**What to listen for:** the silences being the length they are written. Count through them.

**Practice.** Play the first eight bars of a slow piece at the marked tempo, as quietly as you can manage evenly, with the metronome. Then without it, and check you have not drifted faster.
Learning from a video, without becoming:
There is an enormous amount of free piano teaching on video, much of it excellent. There is also a way of using it that stops you learning, and the two look similar.

**What video is genuinely good for:**

- **Watching hands.** Fingering, hand position, rotation, how a leap is taken — things a score cannot show and prose struggles with. This is the real value.
- **Hearing the piece properly played**, once, before you start.
- **A second explanation** when a written one has not landed.
- **Specific technical fixes** — Paul Barton on a particular passage, Hoffman on a particular motion.

**What it is bad for: learning the notes.** A tutorial that shows you which keys to press, bar by bar, teaches the piece and does not teach you to read. Done repeatedly it produces a player who can play twelve pieces and cannot learn a thirteenth without a video.

**Falling-note videos — Synthesia-style — are the extreme case.** No notation, no rhythm notation, no fingering, no shape. They are efficient at getting one piece into the hands and they transfer nothing. Avoid them for anything you intend to learn properly.

**The rule for this curriculum: score first, video second.** Read the piece, mark it up, work out your own fingering, start learning it. Then watch a tutorial and see what you got wrong. That order keeps reading as the primary skill and uses the video for what it is best at.

**The watch-once rule.** Once at the start, once when stuck, once at the end. Watching before every practice session means you are following rather than playing.

**Resources worth the time:** Paul Barton for the standard repertoire, played slowly with the hands visible. Hoffman Academy for technique and for the beginner course. Andrew Furmanczyk's free course for theory and technique.

**Playing along with a recording** is a separate and useful thing: it forces steady time and it teaches you to keep going. Do it once a piece is learned, not while learning it.

**What to listen for:** your own playing rather than the video. If you cannot practise a passage without watching the video first, the passage is not learned.

**Practice.** Take a passage you already play. Watch a tutorial of it and note two differences — fingering, or a motion, or a dynamic. Then close the video and work on one of them.
Playing a cover from a lead sheet:
The chord strand, used for real. Not an arrangement someone else wrote — a chord chart and your own two hands.

**What a lead sheet gives you**: the melody, or sometimes just the words, with chord symbols above. Everything else is yours. Ultimate Guitar has chords for nearly every popular song and they work at a piano unchanged.

**The simplest version that sounds like music:**

1. **Left hand plays the chord root**, on the beat where the chord changes.
2. **Right hand plays the chord**, in whatever inversion is nearest.
3. **Sing or hum the melody.**

That is playable on a chart you have never seen before, in about a minute, and it is the thing most non-classical pianists are actually doing.

**Then make it better, in this order:**

- **Inversions in the right hand**, so the chords move by a step or two instead of jumping. Stage 2's voice-leading.
- **A left-hand pattern** instead of single roots: root–fifth, or a broken chord, or root then chord.
- **The melody in the right hand** with the chord underneath it, in the same hand — which is stage 3's voicing, and the point at which it stops being accompaniment and becomes a piano arrangement.
- **A bass line that moves**, walking between roots.

**Transposing a chart is trivial** and it is why this is worth having: the chords are symbols, so a chart in D♭ becomes a chart in C by rewriting eleven symbols. Stage 4's transposing lesson, used in anger.

**The common progressions do most of the work.** I–V–vi–IV, vi–IV–I–V, I–vi–IV–V, and the minor-key i–VI–III–VII. A very large share of popular music is one of those four, which means that learning them in a few keys makes hundreds of songs playable immediately.

**This is the fastest route to playing for other people**, and it is worth having for that reason alone. Nobody at a party asks for a sonatina.

**What to listen for:** the chord changes landing exactly where the words change. A chord half a beat late is the one error that makes this sound amateur.

**Practice.** Pick a song you like with three or four chords. Get its chart. Play roots in the left hand and chords in the right, through the whole song, twice. Then again with the chords inverted to move smoothly. Then try it a tone higher.
Arranging a song for two hands:
Taking a song you know and making a piano version of it yourself. This is the first lesson where you are the arranger, and it is the foundation of the writing strand later.

**The ingredients you already have**: a melody, chord symbols, and the textures from stage 3 — block chords, broken chords, melody over either.

**The standard arrangement, and it works for almost anything:**

- **Right hand: the melody**, with chord notes filled in underneath where the hand is free.
- **Left hand: the harmony**, as a pattern — root–fifth, root–chord, or a broken chord figure.

**Choose the left-hand pattern from the song's feel.** A ballad takes broken chords; something driving takes root–fifth on the beat; something gentle takes a single held bass note. One pattern for the whole song is fine and is what most published easy arrangements do.

**Decide the key by what fits the hand**, not by the original recording. A song in B major transposes to C or G and nothing is lost. If you intend to sing it, the key is decided by your voice instead.

**Where the melody is too high or too low**, move it an octave. Where the chords are too wide, drop a note — the third and the root are the two that matter, the fifth can go.

**Work out the form first.** Intro, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus. Write the bar count and the chords for each section on paper before playing. An arrangement with no plan becomes the first verse played five times.

**Make the sections different.** Same chords, different texture: verse with single bass notes, chorus with broken chords and the melody doubled an octave up. That contrast is most of what makes an arrangement sound arranged.

**Write it down**, even roughly — chord symbols and bar lines on paper is enough, full notation if you want to use MuseScore's free editor. An arrangement not written down is forgotten in a fortnight.

**Start with a song with four chords and a strong tune.** Anything folk, anything 1960s, most anime endings, most game themes.

**What to listen for:** whether the melody is clearly on top. Self-made arrangements fail here most often, because the arranger knows the tune and cannot hear that it is buried.

**Practice.** Choose a song with four chords. Write its form and chords on paper. Play the melody alone, right hand. Then add a left-hand pattern. Then play it through twice, with a different texture the second time.
Finding an arrangement at the right diff:
The shelf — anime, games, film, pop — is mostly community arrangements, and choosing well among them is a skill of its own.

**MuseScore is the main source.** Several arrangements of most popular songs, at different levels, uploaded by anyone. Free to view in the browser; downloading or printing some of them wants an account or a subscription.

**How to judge an arrangement, with the score open:**

1. **Count the notes in a bar.** An arrangement that stacks four notes per hand throughout is a concert arrangement regardless of its label.
2. **Check the fastest value against the tempo**, as always.
3. **Look for the octave leaps and the hand crossings.** Easy arrangements do not have them.
4. **Check whether the melody is single notes.** Doubled octaves in the melody mean an advanced arrangement.
5. **Read the comments.** Other players say whether it is playable and whether it sounds right.
6. **Prefer well-viewed uploads.** Not a guarantee of quality, but a filter against transcription errors.

**Labels to distrust**: "easy", "beginner", "very easy". They mean the uploader found it easy. Labels to trust slightly more: an explicit grade, or "simplified" in the title.

**Red flags for a bad transcription** rather than a hard one: no dynamics at all, no phrasing marks, bar after bar of identical rhythm, and a key signature that does not match the song you know.

**Two arrangements of the same song is the ideal.** Learn the simpler one now, keep the harder one for later. That is also the honest shape of the shelf: "Merry-Go-Round of Life" at grade 2 now and the real arrangement in a couple of years is not a compromise, it is a route.

**The easiest gateway pieces**, which are genuinely playable at this stage:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Zelda's Lullaby** · **Song of Storms** | few notes, instantly recognisable |
| **Minecraft — Wet Hands**, **Sweden** | slow, simple, atmospheric |
| **Undertale — Fallen Down**, **Home** | easy; Megalovania is not |
| **Howl's Moving Castle — Merry-Go-Round of Life** | at a simplified level |
| **Evangelion — Cruel Angel's Thesis** | chord-chart friendly |
| **Yiruma — River Flows in You** | the classic, and easier than it sounds |

**What to listen for:** whether the arrangement sounds like the song when you play it slowly. A bad transcription does not, and it is not your playing.

**Practice.** Pick a song off your shelf. Find three arrangements of it. Judge them on the six checks and choose one. Then read its first eight bars.
Anime openings, and what makes them hard:
They are a large part of why you want to play, and they are harder than the recordings suggest. This lesson is why, and what to do about it.

**Four things make them difficult:**

1. **Tempo.** Openings are fast — 150 to 180 is normal — and a melody in quavers at 170 is semiquavers at 85. Fast is the single biggest obstacle and it is a stage 6 problem.
2. **Syncopation.** The melodies sit off the beat constantly, which is harder to read and harder to count than almost anything in classical teaching repertoire.
3. **Keys.** Written for voices and guitars, so four and five accidentals are common, and modulations up a semitone for the final chorus are a genre convention.
4. **They are arrangements of band tracks.** The piano version has to carry a vocal line, a guitar, a bass and drums, so even honest arrangements are dense.

**What to do, in order of usefulness:**

- **Take a simplified arrangement** and do not apologise for it. The tune is the tune.
- **Learn it under tempo and stay there** until it is clean. A clean version at 70 per cent is a performance; a scrambled one at full speed is not.
- **Count the syncopation out loud** rather than feeling it. "One and two and" with the melody's entries named.
- **Transpose if the key is brutal.** A chart in D♭ played in C loses nothing a listener will notice.
- **Use the chord-chart route** for songs you want to play rather than study. A chart plus the tune by ear is often better than a bad transcription.

**The pentatonic note.** A lot of Japanese melodic writing uses pentatonic scales — the *yo* and *in* scales — which is why these tunes are often easy to pick out by ear and sound right over simple chords. Stage 9 makes that systematic; it is already usable.

**Candidates that are actually approachable** in simplified arrangements: *Cruel Angel's Thesis*, *Gurenge* (slow version), *Unravel* (the piano intro alone is worth learning), *Again* from Fullmetal Alchemist, and almost any ending theme — endings are slower than openings by convention.

**Keep one on the go at all times**, alongside the classical pieces. It is the thing that keeps the practice voluntary.

**What to listen for:** the rhythm, not the notes. In this genre a wrong note passes unnoticed and a wrong rhythm makes the song unrecognisable.

**Practice.** Choose an opening or ending you want. Find a simplified arrangement. Clap its melody's rhythm, counting aloud, before playing a note. Then learn the first eight bars at a tempo where they are clean.
The textures covers are made of:
Non-classical piano playing uses a small set of accompaniment textures. Learn them as shapes and most of the shelf becomes playable without a transcription.

**1. Root and chord.** Left hand plays the bass note on beat one, then the chord on beats two and three — the oldest and most useful pattern there is. Works for anything in three or four time at a moderate tempo.

**2. Root and fifth.** Bass note, then the fifth above it, alternating. Open, strong, no third, so it fits major or minor. This is the driving pattern for anything rock-shaped.

**3. Broken chord, continuous.** One note per beat or per half-beat, cycling 1–5–3–5. Stage 3's texture; the default for ballads and for most film writing.

**4. Repeated chords.** The whole chord struck on every beat or every half-beat, quietly. Sounds like a string section and is how a great many anime arrangements fill the space under a tune.

**5. Octave melody.** The right hand plays the tune in both the thumb and the fifth finger, an octave apart. Instantly bigger, costs nothing in notes, and it is how you make a chorus sound like a chorus.

**6. Syncopated chords.** The chord played off the beat — on the "and" — while the bass note stays on it. This is the one that makes a cover sound like a record rather than a hymn, and it takes real rhythmic independence.

**7. The held bass with pedal.** Stage 6, and the one that opens up most of what is left.

**Make the sections different, using these.** Verse with pattern 1, chorus with 4 and 5, bridge with 3. Same chords throughout, and it sounds arranged.

**All of them are practised the same way**: left hand alone until automatic by the talking test, then melody over it, then the melody in a different rhythm.

**Where this leads.** Textures plus a chord chart plus the tune by ear is the whole of playing by ear, which is stage 9. You are building the parts now.

**What to listen for:** the texture staying underneath. Every one of these fails the same way, by becoming the loudest thing in the bar.

**Practice.** Take a four-chord song. Play it through with texture 1, then again with 2, then 3, then 4. Two minutes each. Then play its chorus with the melody in octaves.
Playing along with a recording:
The only honest substitute for an ensemble, and the strongest time-keeping exercise there is. It also replaces the one thing a metronome cannot teach.

**What it does that a metronome does not.** A metronome gives you the beat. A recording gives you the beat plus the harmony, the phrasing, the dynamics and the arrival points — so you are not keeping time against a click, you are keeping your place in music.

**How to use it:**

1. **Learn the piece first.** This is not a learning tool, it is a finishing tool.
2. **Find a recording at a tempo you can play.** For classical, there are usually several on YouTube at different speeds; for the shelf, the original track.
3. **Play along, and do not stop.** When you fall out, find the next landmark — the start of the next phrase — and come back in. That skill is the point of the exercise.
4. **Then play along with the piece's own structure in mind**, matching the recording's dynamics and timing rather than just its beat.

**Slowing a recording down is legitimate and easy.** YouTube's playback speed at 0.75 keeps the pitch and makes nearly anything playable along with. Work up by steps.

**Why "do not stop" matters so much.** Practising alone, stopping to fix things is correct. Playing with other music, stopping is the one thing you cannot do — and the habit of continuing through a mistake is what separates a player who can be listened to from one who cannot.

**For classical, use it sparingly.** Matching a recording's rubato exactly is copying an interpretation, and at some point your own timing matters more. Use it for pulse and for the no-stopping discipline, not as the final word on how the piece goes.

**For the shelf, use it constantly.** A cover is supposed to fit the record.

**One honest caveat about your piano.** It is slightly out of tune, so against a recording there will be a small sourness. It is not your playing and it does not affect anything this exercise teaches. If it bothers you, it is an argument for a tuning rather than against the exercise.

**What to listen for:** whether you arrive at the start of each phrase with the recording. Mid-phrase drift matters much less.

**Practice.** Take a piece you have finished. Find a recording, set it to 0.75 speed, and play along once without stopping. Then at full speed, and note where you fell out.
Practising a hard bar: the tools:
Every piece has one or two bars that resist. This lesson is the toolkit, in the order to reach for it.

**First, diagnose. Name the fault.** Not "this bar is hard" — "the fourth finger is late", "the hands are not together on beat three", "the leap lands short". Everything below depends on having named it.

**The tools:**

1. **Slower.** Halve the tempo. If it is not clean at half speed, the problem is not speed.
2. **Hands separately.** Each hand alone until automatic by the talking test. Most hands-together faults are a hands-separate fault in disguise.
3. **Review the fingering.** A bar that will not work very often has a fingering problem, and changing it fixes in a day what repetition would not fix in a month. This is the first thing to check, not the last.
4. **Backward chaining.** Last two notes, then three, then four, always ending somewhere secure.
5. **Fragment it.** Two notes — just the transition that fails — twenty times, slowly, watching the hand.
6. **Change the rhythm.** Play the passage with the first of each pair long and the second short, then the reverse. Both versions expose different unevenness and together they fix it.
7. **Add a note.** Play the bar plus one note of the next bar, so the hand learns to leave rather than to stop.
8. **Block it.** Play all the notes of each beat together as a chord, to see the hand positions without the rhythm. Then restore the rhythm.
9. **Mental play.** Away from the piano, imagine the bar note by note with the fingering. If you cannot, you do not know it yet, and this is the cheapest way to find that out.
10. **Leave it and come back tomorrow.** Overnight consolidation is real and twenty minutes of grinding at the end of a session makes a bar worse.

**Do not play the whole piece to get to the hard bar.** Every run-through practises the hard bar once and the easy bars twenty times, which is the wrong ratio.

**Cap it at ten minutes a session.** A bar that has had ten focused minutes has had what it can use today.

**What to listen for:** the named fault, and only that.

**Practice.** Take the hardest bar of your current piece. Name the fault out loud. Then work through tools 3, 2, 5 and 6 on it, five minutes total. Then play the section it sits in, once.
Fixing a piece you learned wrong:
It will happen, and the fix is specific. A wrong note learned at forty repetitions does not come out with the forty-first.

**How it happens.** A note misread on day one, a fingering invented differently each session, a rhythm learned by ear from a recording that does not match the page. By the time it is noticed, the error has been practised into the hand along with everything else.

**Why repetition alone does not fix it.** The wrong version is a learned movement. Playing the passage again mostly rehearses the stronger memory — which is the wrong one. Under pressure, the wrong version is what comes out.

**The fix, and it is not more repetitions:**

1. **Stop playing the passage at all** for a day or two. Breaking the chain matters.
2. **Re-read the bar from the score as though it were new.** Note names out loud. Rhythm counted aloud.
3. **Decide the correct fingering and write it in.**
4. **Learn it as a new fragment**, extremely slowly, hands separately — the full learning sequence on two bars.
5. **Rebuild the joins** into and out of it, as separate fragments.
6. **Only then** play the section, slowly, and only once or twice per session for a week.

**It takes roughly three times as long as learning it right would have.** That is the real argument for marking up a score and settling the fingering before learning anything.

**The commonest ones to check for**, when something feels unreliable: an accidental from the key signature missed in one octave, a dotted rhythm flattened to even notes, a tied note released early, and a fingering that changes depending on how the previous bar went.

**Rhythm errors are the hardest to hear in your own playing** because the wrong version sounds normal once learned. Count aloud against the score, or clap the written rhythm while reading, and the discrepancy appears.

**The prevention is cheap.** Read it right on day one, finger it once and write it down, count the rhythm out loud before playing it. Ten minutes at the start against a week later on.

**What to listen for:** the passage sounding slightly different each time you play it. That is unsettled fingering, and it is the earliest warning you get.

**Practice.** Take a piece you have played for a while and read one page of it carefully against the score, naming notes and counting rhythm aloud. Expect to find something — most players do.
Keeping pieces alive:
A finished piece decays. Without a system, you arrive at a year of playing with no pieces you can actually play, which is the standard self-taught predicament.

**Keep a written list.** Three columns is enough:

| State | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Learning** | currently being worked on. Two or three at most. |
| **Playable** | finished, and still comes out right. Needs a run-through now and then. |
| **Lapsed** | finished once, no longer reliable. Can be revived in a fraction of the original time. |

**Rotate the playable ones.** One or two per session, played through once, for pleasure rather than for improvement. Five minutes.

**That is also the warm-up.** A session that begins with a piece you can play is a better start than scales, and it means the repertoire maintains itself as a side effect.

**Reviving a lapsed piece is fast** — days rather than weeks — if it was properly finished. If it was never properly finished it comes back as badly as it was, which is the practical argument for the stage's rule.

**Expect three to five pieces to be genuinely playable at any time.** That is normal for an amateur and it is plenty. Professionals keep more because they play more hours, not because they forget less.

**Which to keep playable:** the ones you would play if asked. One short classical piece, one slow atmospheric thing, one off the shelf. That set covers nearly every situation in which anyone will ever ask you to play.

**Write the fingerings and the markings in the score properly**, once, for anything going onto the playable list. A revived piece with an unmarked score is relearned from scratch.

**Do not keep everything.** A piece you no longer like is allowed to lapse. The list is a tool, not a record.

**What to listen for, in a revived piece:** the hard bar. It is the first thing to go and the first thing to check.

**Practice.** Write the list today, with what you have. Then play one piece from the playable column, start to end, for pleasure — no fixing, no stopping.
Polishing: what makes a piece finished:
The gap between playing the notes and playing the piece. This lesson is the checklist for closing it.

**Finished means all of this:**

- **Start to end without stopping**, three times out of four.
- **At a tempo that sounds like the music.** Not necessarily the printed one — but not so slow that the shape disappears.
- **No bar you dread.** A single feared bar means the piece is not finished, however well the rest goes.
- **Fingering settled and identical every time.**
- **Phrasing in it** — each line shaped, with a breath at the end.
- **Dynamics in it**, written and implied.
- **Balance** — the melody above the accompaniment, throughout.
- **The rhythm honest.** Dotted notes dotted, rests full length, no rushing the difficult bar and resting on the easy one.
- **Recoverable.** When something goes wrong you keep going, and a listener cannot tell where.

**Polishing is its own phase and it takes about as long as learning the notes.** Most amateur playing stops at the point where the notes are learned, which is why most amateur playing sounds like practising.

**Work on one item per session.** Today, dynamics only. Tomorrow, phrasing only. The day after, start-to-end runs only. Trying to polish everything at once polishes nothing.

**The run-through is practice too.** Play it start to end, note where it broke, then go and fix that one thing in fragments — not by running it again. Repeated run-throughs are how a stumble gets learned.

**Play it slowly once a week, even when it is finished.** Slow playing is where errors creep back visibly, and it is the standard maintenance tool for the rest of your playing life.

**Then stop.** A piece polished past the point of return starts to go stale and the time is better spent on the next one. You will come back to it in a year and play it better for having left it.

**What to listen for, in the final week:** the piece as a whole — does it go somewhere? That is the only question left once the details are right, and it is the one that makes playing worth listening to.

**Practice.** Take your most finished piece. Play it start to end once. Write down the one thing that was worst. Fix only that, in fragments, for ten minutes. Then leave it until tomorrow.
Memorising a piece on purpose:
Stage 3 covered how memory happens as a by-product. This is doing it deliberately, which is a different and more reliable thing.

**The four memories, and a secure piece uses all of them:**

| Memory | What it is | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Muscle** | the hands know the movement | you stop for any reason mid-piece |
| **Aural** | you know how it sounds next | the room or the piano is different |
| **Visual** | you see the page, or the hands | under pressure |
| **Analytical** | you know the harmony and the form | never, and it is the one most neglected |

**Muscle memory alone is the trap.** It is what you get for free from repetition, it feels like knowing the piece, and it breaks completely at the first interruption — because it runs forwards only and has no entry points.

**So memorise analytically, on purpose:**

1. **Know the form.** Say it out loud: eight bars, repeat, sixteen-bar middle section in the dominant, eight bars back. A piece you can describe you can navigate.
2. **Know the harmony.** Name the chord of each bar, or each phrase. "Bars 9 to 12 are a V going home."
3. **Make entry points.** Four or five places in the piece you can start from cold. Practise starting there. This is what makes a memory lapse survivable rather than terminal.
4. **Mental play.** Away from the piano, play it through in your head with the fingering. Where the image goes blank is exactly where the memory is not there — and that is far cheaper to find at a table than at the keyboard.

**Memorise in sections, from the hardest.** Same order as learning.

**Hands separately, from memory**, is a strong test — much harder than together, because the hands prop each other up.

**Keep the score.** Memorised does not mean finished with the page; go back to it weekly while a piece is new, because memory drifts, and a drifted note is a learned error.

**Not everything needs memorising.** Memorise the two or three pieces on your playable list. Read the rest. Sight-reading and memorising are different skills and a player who only memorises reads badly.

**What to listen for:** hesitation at section joins when playing from memory. That is a missing entry point.

**Practice.** Take a finished piece. Say its form out loud. Name the chord of each phrase. Choose four entry points and play from each one, cold, twice. Then play it through from memory, slowly.
Playing it for someone:
Playing alone and playing while someone listens are different activities, and the difference is learnable rather than a matter of temperament.

**What changes.** Attention narrows, hands get less reliable, tempo goes up, and anything held together by muscle memory alone falls over. Nothing about the piece changed; the conditions did.

**Why it is worth doing anyway.** A piece that survives being heard is genuinely finished. Playing only alone leaves you unable to tell the difference between a piece you can play and one you can nearly play.

**What actually helps**, in order:

1. **Over-prepare, and know it analytically.** The previous lesson is the preparation for this one. Entry points are what turn a lapse into a pause rather than a stop.
2. **Choose a piece below your ceiling.** Whatever you play for someone should be comfortably within what you can do — never your hardest piece.
3. **Practise the beginning more than anything.** The first eight bars carry all the nerves, and a confident opening settles everything after it.
4. **Practise starting.** Sit down, settle the hands, take a breath, begin. Three seconds of stillness before the first note. That ritual is worth rehearsing.
5. **Rehearse continuing.** Deliberately practise playing on through a mistake without reacting. A listener hears a stop; they almost never hear a wrong note.
6. **Play it slightly slower than you can.** Nerves add tempo, so aim below and it lands right.

**Start with one person who likes you.** The jump from alone to an audience of one is most of the distance; the jump from one to five is much less.

**Afterwards, judge one thing only**: did it hold together? Not whether it was perfect. A piece played through with two wrong notes was a success.

**Nerves do not go away and they are not supposed to.** They get familiar, and then they stop being information about whether you can play.

**What to listen for, in the week before:** whether the start-to-end runs are reliable three times out of four. If not, play something else and bring this one back next time.

**Practice.** Pick the most secure piece you have. Practise the first eight bars and the sitting-down ritual. Then play it for one person, once, and continue through whatever happens.
Sight-reading: raising the level:
Four stages in, the daily ten minutes has a new job: it should now be getting harder on purpose.

**The level rule, restated.** Read material you can play at sight — roughly two grades below what you can learn. That has not changed, and it is still the whole point: reading is practised by succeeding, not by struggling.

**But the level moves.** As your playing level rises, so does the reading level, and the commonest failure is reading the same easy hymns for two years because they are comfortable. If today's reading never surprises you, it is too easy.

**How to tell you are at the right level:** you get through a piece at a steady slow tempo, without stopping, with most of the notes right and nearly all the rhythm right. If you are stopping, go easier. If it is effortless, go harder.

**What to add now:**

- **Keys with three and four accidentals**, named before you start.
- **Two staves with real independence** — hymns, chorales, easy Bach.
- **Changes of position**, so the hands must move rather than sit.
- **A wider range of time signatures**, including 6/8 and 3/8.
- **Dynamics and articulation read at sight**, not just pitches and rhythms. This is the step most readers never take, and it is what makes sight-reading musical rather than mechanical.

**Material, free:** the Anna Magdalena Notebook, hymnals, Czerny Op. 599, Burgmüller Op. 100, Streabbog, Gurlitt, and the easier Schumann Op. 68 — all on IMSLP, hundreds of pieces, no repeats needed.

**The habits stay the same.** Name the key. Scan the whole bar before playing it. Eyes a beat ahead. Never stop, never repeat, never fix.

**Four hands is the best version of this exercise** if you ever have someone to play with, because you cannot stop. Failing that, playing along with a recording does some of the same work.

**What it buys you.** At this stage, reading is what decides how much music you get to play. A good reader tries twenty pieces to find the one they want to learn; a poor reader learns whatever they already know how to play.

**What to listen for:** nothing, still. Did you keep going.

**Practice.** Ten minutes, today, on something one notch harder than yesterday — a hymn in four sharps, or a Bach minuet you have not seen. Name the key, scan the first bar, and go.
The five pieces:
The set for this stage, with candidates. Three classical in three styles, two off the shelf, all finished.

**1. Baroque.** Petzold's Minuet in G (BWV Anh. 114) or G minor (Anh. 115), Bach's Little Prelude in C (BWV 939), Bach's Prelude in C (BWV 846).

**2. Classical.** Clementi's Sonatina Op. 36 No. 1 (first or second movement), the Sonatina in G attributed to Beethoven (Anh. 5), Mozart's Minuet in F (K. 2).

**3. Romantic.** Burgmüller's Arabesque or La Candeur (Op. 100), Schumann's Melody or Soldier's March (Op. 68), Tchaikovsky's Old French Song (Op. 39).

**4 and 5. Off the shelf.** One easy and recognisable — a Zelda theme, a Minecraft piece, *River Flows in You* — and one you actually want, in a simplified arrangement: an anime opening or ending, a film theme, a song you like from a chord chart and your own arrangement.

**A recommended set, if you want it chosen for you:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Petzold — Minuet in G minor** | two lines, minor key, finger legato |
| **Clementi — Sonatina Op. 36 No. 1, 1st mvt** | melody over Alberti bass, tempo discipline |
| **Burgmüller — Arabesque, Op. 100 No. 2** | the scales paying off audibly |
| **Satie — Gymnopédie No. 1** | tone, quiet control, and the piece you will play when asked |
| **One anime or game piece of your choosing** | the reason any of this is happening |

**All five at once, interleaved**, at different stages of completion. Not one after another.

**Finish them.** That is the stage. A piece that reaches the polishing checklist and passes it counts; one that is "mostly there" does not.

**Expect three to six months**, and expect the fifth to go much faster than the first. That speed-up is the real output of this stage — not the five pieces, but the fact that the sixth one will take weeks instead of months.

**Write them on the repertoire list** as you finish them, and keep two or three in the playable column.

**What to listen for:** across the five, whether finishing has got easier. It should.

**Practice.** Choose your five today and write them down. Start the Baroque piece and one off the shelf. Add the others as the first ones mature.
What stage 5 was for:
Review, and what stage 6 does.

**What should now be true:**

- Five pieces finished — three classical in three styles, two off the shelf.
- You judge a score's difficulty before committing to it, and you find the hardest bar first.
- You know where the free scores are and which edition to take.
- The learning sequence is a routine rather than a decision: listen, mark up, finger, section, hardest first, hands separately, slowly together, joins, tempo, then the music.
- Backward chaining, rhythm changes, blocking and mental play are tools you reach for by name.
- You can play a song from a chord chart, and you have arranged one yourself.
- You know the seven accompaniment textures and can put a verse and a chorus in different ones.
- You have played along with a recording without stopping.
- You can revive a lapsed piece, and you keep a repertoire list.
- At least one piece is memorised with entry points, not just with muscle memory.
- You have played for one person.
- Sight-reading is harder than it was in stage 4, and still daily.

**What this stage really bought.** Not the five pieces — the fact that learning a piece is now a procedure rather than an adventure. That is the thing that compounds.

**Where you are, honestly.** Roughly grade 2 to 3 in the exam systems, which nobody is asking you to take. More usefully: you can learn most simplified arrangements of music you like, and the easy end of the standard classical repertoire, without help.

**What stage 6 does.** Technique and the pedal — the two things standing between here and intermediate repertoire. Speed, finger independence, Czerny, and the sustain pedal properly: when to put it down, when to lift, and the syncopated pedalling that every Romantic piece assumes. Expect the Romantic and slow pieces from this stage to sound like different music afterwards.

**One warning for that stage.** Technique work is where injuries happen, because it is repetitive and it tempts force. Stage 1's rules about tension, weight and stopping apply more there than anywhere else in this curriculum.

**Practice.** Go down the list. Then play all five pieces, start to end, one after another, for nobody. That is a recital, and you have never been able to do it before.
What technique is for, and the one rule:
Stage 6 is the technical stage, and it opens with the thing that makes it safe.

**Technique is the ability to play something with ease.** That is the whole definition. It is not strength, it is not endurance, and it is not a quantity of exercises completed. A passage is technically secure when it costs you almost nothing to play.

**So the measure of a technical exercise is whether the movement got easier**, not whether you did it fifty times.

**The one rule: force is never the answer.** If a passage needs force, the movement is wrong. Loud playing comes from the arm's weight arriving fast, not from pressing harder; speed comes from efficiency, not effort. Every injury pianists get comes from applying force to a movement that was not working.

**What goes wrong in this stage, specifically.** Technical work is repetitive, measurable and tempting. It is the only part of learning the piano where you can do a thing a hundred times in ten minutes, and a hundred repetitions of a tense movement is how tendinitis starts. The whole of stage 1's body work applies here more than anywhere.

**The four things this stage builds:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The pedal** | the single largest change in how your playing sounds |
| **Speed** | and the honest account of where it comes from |
| **Independence and evenness** | fingers that do not drag each other |
| **The specific shapes** | octaves, thirds, repeated notes, trills, leaps |

**Ten to fifteen minutes of technique a session, maximum**, inside a session that is otherwise music. Technique practised for an hour is an hour of risk for the return of fifteen minutes.

**Czerny, not Hanon.** The argument is in a later lesson and it is not a matter of taste.

**Shake the hands out between items.** Arms hanging, five seconds. Do it every time you change exercise, for the rest of your life.

**What to listen for:** your own breathing. Held breath means held muscles, and it is the earliest sign of effort going into the wrong place.

**Practice.** Play a C major scale, two octaves, hands together, and pay attention to nothing but how much effort it takes. Then play it again, trying to use less. That difference — not the notes — is what this stage works on.
Tension, and the signals to stop:
Stage 1 covered posture and arm weight. This lesson is the maintenance version, and it exists because this is the stage where it matters.

**The checks, done mid-piece without stopping:**

1. **Shoulders.** Down. If they have crept up, drop them and carry on.
2. **Jaw and neck.** Unclenched. People clench their jaws at difficult bars.
3. **Breathing.** Continuous. Held breath is the most reliable tension signal there is.
4. **The wrist.** Level and mobile, not locked. A locked wrist transmits everything to the forearm.
5. **The non-playing hand.** It should be loose. A left hand gripping while the right plays something hard is pure wasted tension.
6. **The fingers not in use.** Lightly curved and still, not braced or lifted high.

**Run the checks at the start of every technical item.** Thirty seconds, from the shoulders down.

**The signals that mean stop now**, not finish the session:

- **Pain anywhere.** Not soreness after unfamiliar work — pain during playing.
- **Tingling or numbness** in the fingers or hands.
- **A forearm that feels pumped or tight**, the way it does after carrying something heavy.
- **Weakness**, or a finger that stops responding.
- **Pain that is still there the next morning.**

**What those can become.** Tendinitis, carpal tunnel syndrome, and in the worst case focal dystonia, which can end playing permanently. All three are overwhelmingly caused by repetitive tense practice, and all three are far easier to avoid than to treat. Nobody is watching you practise, so these rules are the substitute for a teacher's eye.

**Stopping costs nothing.** Two days off repairs an overworked forearm. Two months off repairs an injury. There is no deadline on any of this — *ad astra* has no schedule.

**Warm up, briefly and genuinely.** Five minutes of slow, easy playing before anything technical. Cold hands and fast repetitions are the worst combination available.

**Take a break every twenty to thirty minutes.** Stand up, drop the arms, move. Long unbroken sessions are where accumulated tension turns into something.

**What to listen for:** the sound getting harder and more percussive as a session goes on. That is tension becoming audible, and it means the session is over.

**Practice.** Run the six checks now, at the keyboard, playing something easy. Note which one you failed — most people fail the shoulders or the breathing — and check that one at every session for a fortnight.
The pedals on your piano — and what the:
Before any pedalling technique: find out what your piano actually has. It is a century-old upright, and uprights differ from the grands that every tutorial is filmed on.

**The right pedal is the sustain pedal**, sometimes called the damper pedal. Press it and every damper lifts off the strings, so notes keep ringing after you release the keys. This one does the work and the next several lessons are about it.

**The left pedal is the soft pedal.** On a grand it shifts the whole action sideways so the hammers strike two strings instead of three — *una corda*. On an upright it does something different: it moves the hammers closer to the strings, so they have less distance to travel and strike with less force. Quieter and slightly duller, with none of the colour change a grand gives.

**The middle pedal, if you have one, is the question.** On a grand it is the sostenuto, which holds only the notes you are already playing. On uprights it is usually one of:

- **A practice mute** — a strip of felt drops between hammers and strings, making the piano very quiet and rather horrible. Common on older uprights and genuinely useful if you want to play late.
- **A bass sustain** — sustains only the lower half of the keyboard.
- **Nothing at all**, or a duplicate of the soft pedal.

**Find out which yours is.** Hold a low note's key down, press the middle pedal, release the key, and listen: if the note continues, it is a bass sustain or a sostenuto. Press it alone and play: if the whole piano goes soft and muffled, it is a practice mute.

**Then write it down somewhere**, because every tutorial you watch will assume a grand and be wrong about your instrument.

**A century-old action has consequences.** The pedal may be noisy, may have a long travel, and may not release cleanly at the top. Listen for a thump when you lift, and for notes continuing slightly after a full lift — a damper not seating properly. Neither is your technique.

**That is also the first item on the tuning-and-regulation list.** The piano plays nicely and is slightly out of tune; a technician would also check damper seating, and it matters more for pedalling than for anything else.

**What to listen for:** the pedal's own mechanical noise. On an old upright it can be audible, and learning to move the foot slowly and quietly is part of the technique.

**Practice.** Identify all your pedals by the tests above. Then play a single low note, hold the sustain pedal, and listen to how long the note actually lasts. That length is a property of your piano and it decides how you will pedal on it.
The sustain pedal: what it actually does:
Most people treat the pedal as a loudness knob. It is a damper lift, and understanding that is what separates pedalling from smearing.

**The mechanism.** Every string has a felt damper resting on it. A key press lifts that one damper; the pedal lifts all of them at once. Notes already sounding keep sounding, and notes played while the pedal is down keep sounding after you release the keys.

**Three things happen, not one:**

1. **Notes continue** after the fingers leave them. This is the obvious one.
2. **The whole instrument resonates.** With all dampers off, strings you did not play vibrate in sympathy with the ones you did. The piano gets richer, warmer and noticeably louder.
3. **The attack changes.** A note played with the dampers up blooms differently from the same note played dry.

**Which is why it is not a loudness control.** It is a colour and connection control that happens to also add loudness.

**What it is actually for, in order of importance:**

- **Connecting notes the hand cannot connect.** A bass note held under a chord the hand has left. This is the main use and it is why Romantic piano writing is physically possible.
- **Richness.** The sympathetic resonance, used deliberately.
- **Letting a chord ring** past where the fingers must leave it.

**What it is not for:** covering gaps caused by not having learned the notes. Pedal over an unlearned passage sounds exactly like pedal over an unlearned passage.

**The cost: mud.** Two different harmonies held together with the pedal clash, and the longer the pedal is down the more of the piece is sounding at once. Every pedalling decision is a trade between connection and clarity.

**On your piano, specifically.** An old upright with slightly loose tuning gets muddier faster than a well-tuned grand, because the sympathetic strings are not quite in agreement. You will need to pedal somewhat more sparingly than a recording suggests, and that is the instrument talking, not you.

**The honest beginner default is less pedal, not more.** Dry playing with clear notes sounds like a learner being careful. Mud sounds like a learner who cannot hear.

**What to listen for:** the moment the sound stops being one harmony. That is the moment the pedal should have come up.

**Practice.** Play a C major chord, pedal down, and listen until it dies. Then play C major, then F major, then G major, slowly, with the pedal held down through all three — and listen to the mud. That is what the next lessons prevent.
The foot: down, up, and silently:
The physical technique, which takes about a week to make automatic and is then invisible for the rest of your life.

**The foot position.** Heel on the floor, the ball of the foot on the pedal, the foot staying in contact with the pedal at all times. The ankle hinges; the leg does not lift.

**Keep contact even when the pedal is up.** Lifting the foot off and putting it back on is how you get a thump, and it makes the timing of the next press imprecise.

**Which foot.** The right, for the sustain pedal, always — the left stays flat on the floor as part of your balance. If you are using both pedals, the left foot takes the left pedal.

**Move slowly at both ends.** A pedal slammed down makes a mechanical noise and lifts the dampers with a thud; a pedal released fast makes the dampers land on the strings audibly. Both are clearly audible on an old upright. Press and release through the travel, not at it.

**Find the exact point where the dampers lift.** It is partway through the pedal's travel, not at the bottom. Play a note, press the pedal very slowly, and feel and hear where it engages. Everything about control lives around that point, and finding it is the single most useful thing in this lesson.

**You do not need the full travel.** Most pedalling happens in a small range around the engagement point. Pushing to the floor every time is wasted motion and makes the next change slower.

**Sit so the foot can reach without changing your posture.** If pedalling tips you forward or makes you slide, the bench is too close or too far. Fix the bench, not the leg.

**Watch the knee, not the foot.** Looking down at the pedal pulls the head and spine out of position, and you cannot see the engagement point anyway. The foot learns by feel within days.

**One shoe note.** Pedal in shoes with a thin, firm sole, or barefoot — whichever you will do consistently. Thick soft soles hide the engagement point.

**What to listen for:** your pedal's own noise. If you can hear the mechanism, the foot is moving too fast.

**Practice.** Play one note. Press the pedal slowly until the note's tail appears, and stop there. Release just as slowly. Twenty times, listening only for mechanical noise. Then find the engagement point without playing anything — purely by feel.
Syncopated pedalling:
The one pedalling technique that matters most. Learn it and the pedal stops smearing; miss it and nothing else in this stage helps.

**The problem it solves.** You are playing a bass note under a chord, and you need to move the hand. Hold the pedal and the old harmony stays when the new one arrives: mud. Lift the pedal with the new chord and there is a gap: the connection breaks.

**The solution: change the pedal just after the new note sounds.** Play the chord, then immediately lift and re-press the pedal. The old sound is cut by the lift, the new one is caught by the press, and the join is seamless.

**So the foot is always a fraction behind the hand.** That is why it is called syncopated — or legato — pedalling, and it is backwards from what everyone does instinctively.

**The sequence, counted:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Beat 1** | play the chord — pedal is still down from before |
| **Just after** | lift the pedal, then press it again |
| **Beat 2, 3, 4** | pedal stays down, hand free to move |
| **Next beat 1** | play the next chord, then change again |

**Say it as "play, then change".** Not "change, then play".

**How to learn it, and this works in about a week:**

1. **Chords with no pedal first.** C, F, G, C, one per bar, left hand, at 60.
2. **Then add the pedal change** after each chord, deliberately late — a clear fraction after the note.
3. **Then tighten** the gap until the change is immediately after, and inaudible.
4. **Then with the hands leaving the keys**, so the pedal is genuinely doing the connecting. Play the chord, lift the hand entirely, and the sound should continue unbroken.

**That last step is the test.** If lifting the hand produces silence or a bump, the change was too early or too late.

**Where the change goes in real music: with the harmony.** Each new chord gets a change. In slow pieces that is every beat or two; in a fast piece, much less often.

**What to listen for:** a gap, or an overlap. Both are audible at slow tempo and both disappear with a week of this exercise.

**Practice.** Left hand, C–F–G–C, one chord per bar at 60, with a pedal change after each. Lift the hand off between chords and listen for the join. Ten times. Then the same on your current piece's chord changes.
Reading pedal marks, and why they are su:
How pedalling is written, and the thing nobody tells beginners: most of what you see was added by an editor.

**The notations:**

- **Ped.** followed by a line, with an asterisk ✱ or a bracket end where it lifts. The older style.
- **A horizontal bracket** under the staff, with a V-shaped notch where the pedal changes without fully releasing. The modern style, and more precise.
- **Nothing at all**, which is extremely common — including in a great deal of music that needs pedal.

**Where the marks come from.** Beethoven and after wrote some pedalling themselves, and it is musically important when they did. But most printed pedalling in cheap editions is editorial — added by a nineteenth or twentieth-century editor, often without being marked as an addition. Chopin's own pedalling is detailed and worth following; the pedalling in a 1900 teaching edition of Chopin may be someone else's entirely.

**Hence the rule: pedal marks are information, not instruction.** Follow them first, then judge them by ear on your instrument, in your room.

**Why your instrument matters.** Pedalling that is right on a modern grand in a dry room can be mud on an old upright in a small room, and the reverse. A composer's pedalling was written for a piano whose notes died far faster than yours.

**A composer's own pedalling is different, though.** Where a score says the mark is the composer's — good editions say so — treat it as part of the piece. Beethoven's long pedals are deliberate blurs and taking them literally is the point.

**Baroque scores have no pedal marks because there was no pedal.** Any pedalling in a Bach edition is editorial, and usually best ignored.

**Write your own in**, in pencil, once you have decided. Pedalling worked out and not written down gets re-decided every session, like fingering.

**The shorthand worth adopting:** a line under the bars where the pedal is down, with a notch at each change. It takes seconds and it is unambiguous.

**What to listen for:** whether the printed pedalling muddies your piano. If it does, yours is right and the edition is not wrong — it was written for a different room.

**Practice.** Take a Romantic piece you are learning. Find its pedal marks, play one phrase following them exactly, then play it again with your own pedalling by ear. Keep whichever is clearer and pencil it in.
Pedalling by ear: listening for mud:
The actual skill. The notation is a guide, the technique is mechanical, and everything that is left is a listening decision made several times a bar.

**The question, every time: is more than one harmony sounding?** If yes, change the pedal. That is the whole rule, and applying it is harder than it sounds because you are also playing.

**Where the pedal changes, in order of reliability:**

1. **At every change of harmony.** The default, and right most of the time.
2. **At the bass note**, when the bass is moving — the bass is what defines the harmony, so a new bass usually wants a change.
3. **Before a rest**, so the silence is silent.
4. **At phrase ends**, with the breath.
5. **Never in the middle of a scale run**, unless you want a wash.

**The passing-note exception.** A melody note that is not in the chord — a scale note on its way somewhere — does not need its own pedal change. Changing for every melody note would mean changing constantly and losing the connection the pedal is there to make. Change with the harmony, not with the tune.

**Listening while playing is the difficulty.** Most people pedal by rule and never hear the result. Two fixes:

- **Play a phrase with your eyes shut** and attend only to the sound, not to whether the pedalling matched the plan.
- **Play it with no pedal at all**, then with pedal, back to back. The comparison makes mud obvious in a way that pedalling alone does not.

**Be more sparing in the bass.** Low notes have long, strong decays and muddy much faster than high ones. The same pedalling that is clear in the treble is thick two octaves down, and this is where your piano's slight tuning drift shows most.

**Louder means shorter.** A loud chord holds more sound, so it needs changing sooner. A quiet passage can take much longer pedals.

**Your room counts.** A small hard room adds its own reverberation to the piano's. Pedalling learned from headphones on a recording transfers badly.

**What to listen for:** the bass. It is almost always the first thing to turn muddy and the last thing a learner notices.

**Practice.** Take eight bars of a slow piece. Play them with no pedal, then with a change at every harmony, then with a change at every bass note. Choose by ear, and pencil it in.
Half pedal, and partial lifts:
The pedal is not a switch, and the middle of its travel is where control lives.

**What a partial lift does.** Raise the dampers part-way and they touch the strings lightly: the sound is damped but not cut, so a held harmony loses its thickness without losing its continuity. Low notes, with their heavy strings, keep ringing longest, which is exactly what you usually want.

**So the three positions are down, part-way, and up** — and the part-way one is a continuous range rather than a point.

**Where it is used:**

- **Thinning a long pedal** without breaking it, in a slow passage where a full change would be audible.
- **Managing the bass** in music that holds a bass note through changing harmonies.
- **Clearing a run** while keeping the harmony underneath, at the end of a phrase.

**The flutter pedal** is the other partial technique: several rapid small lifts, used to clear a loud, dense sound progressively — typically through a long diminuendo, or at the end of a big passage. It sounds like one continuous thinning rather than a series of changes.

**It is instrument-dependent and that matters here.** How much partial lift you need, and how well it works, depends on how the dampers are regulated. On a hundred-year-old upright the damper felts may not lift perfectly evenly, so the half-pedal range may be narrower or less reliable than on a grand. Find yours by experiment rather than by what a video says.

**Do not reach for this yet in a piece.** Full changes done well cover almost everything in the repertoire of this stage and the next. Half-pedalling is the refinement you add when a full change is audibly wrong and no pedal is audibly worse.

**How to find your piano's range.** Play a loud low octave with the pedal down. Then raise the pedal very slowly, in stages, listening at each. You will hear the sound thin before it stops. The usable range is between those two points, and on some uprights it is small.
